rv.q: So much modern theatre is po-faced, palsied by political correctness. Not this.
The 47th is an imagination of a future world.

But really, it's tremendous entertainment, that explores the decline of American democracy in an infinitely more enjoyable way than the actual decline of American democracy we must all bear witness to.
Most marvellously, Trump's bonkers, bite-size Twitter philosophy is a perfect fit with Bartlett's modern take on Shakespearean verse.
But it’s gripping, funny, restless and ambitious, diving into the terrifying problem of leaders prepared to tear up democracy for their own ends (the play’s title has a twist).

Bertie Carvel’s Trump is alone worth the price of a ticket: not so much an impersonation as a reincarnation, as if Carvel himself has completely vanished and in his place something that seems barely human – a wax model perhaps – has been given palpable life.
The language and staging of The 47th is eloquent and clever, but it has surprisingly little to say about a monster so huge.
But the drama looks and feels like a conceptual riff rather than truly Shakespearean in its effects.
It's Carvel who leaves the biggest impression, bestriding the production in a magnificent and grimly apposite fashion.
It’s cartoonish fun, but it doesn’t offer much more to chew on than a Spitting Image sketch.
Goold brings his usual sheen to proceedings, yet can't hide the lack of meaningful substance beneath the theatrical polish.
The debate that unfolds is both fascinating and frightening, given more weight by the blank verse.
This is a performance that in itself makes this show worth seeing.
Rupert Goold’s direction is slick and not a minute is wasted.
Bartlett’s audacity — plus the fact that Tunie, Wilson and especially Carvel never relinquish their grip on the audience — makes “The 47th” rarely less than entertaining.
That said, The 47th is certainly provocative, with a remarkable performance at its center from Bertie Carvel, seen recently as Banquo in Joel Coen’s The Tragedy of Macbeth.
Bertie Carvel, whose portrayal of Trump is the play’s banner achievement, is first seen chugging into view on a golf cart: an impressive entrance that starts the play on a high.

This is a never less than high energy production in which Bertie Carvel gives the performance of his career; but like the golf ball he strikes across the stage in the opening scene, the satire doesn’t entirely hit its target.
Ultimately, Bartlett’s play, though vastly entertaining, neither offers fresh wisdom on the past nor grapples with the future; there’s no mention of Covid or Ukraine.
It’s a shame that this promising play is so detached from its subject-matter but the creative team have decided to write about US politics without reading about it.
The 47th isn't the most enlightening of works and has clear issues in its tone and endgame, but it's exceptionally entertaining.
This production comes at you; like Trump is unbound.

Inevitably, there is further civil unrest, led by the Shaman (Joss Carter), and Harris has to deal with the fallout. The political ambitions of Trump’s daughter Ivanka (Lydia Wilson, also superb) are ramped up by Bartlett – the consequences terrifying to contemplate.

It's a playful fever dream about the corrosive impact of populism and social media on democracy, featuring a grotesquely lifelike turn by Bertie Carvel as the orange-hued panto villain who rocks up in a golf buggy with the taunt: "I know you hate me."
That said, this is still a good production, worth seeing for Carvel and Tunie’s performances alone.

cn.t: Carvel's transformative Trump performance electrifies Bartlett's ambitious Shakespearean satire, but critics are divided on whether the blank-verse political fantasy matches the brilliance of its lead—some find it gripping, others hollow spectacle.
